doc.title: Benny Powell interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Artist versus entertainer and sidemen
summary: Discussion of artists versus entertainers, sidemen as artists, and Powell's National Endowment panel experience, with Woods on pay and accountability.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: That’s another thing I wanted to ask you about. The concept, the difference between, as we know it today with pop culture, the difference between an artist and an entertainer. Because when I look at some of the earlier great jazz musicians, to me they were both. What they did it was art, it was beautiful, it was so beautifully constructed, and yet it was entertaining. And now it seems like we have entertainers that get paid exorbitant amounts of money to sing or play about things that don’t have much merit. There is so much raunchiness in today’s music. And to me jazz is a more beautiful form of expression that runs closer to the authenticity of art. Could you talk about that for a moment? Well contrast or compare some of your own experiences.

Well it’s a little more sophisticated. And I think lazy people don’t like jazz because they don’t want to take the time to really find out anything about it. How can I address that? Well it made me think of one thing, and I’ll come back to your question. But one time I had to deal with sidemen versus artists. Or getting sidemen to look at themselves like artists. Sidemen might be just a person like myself. I was in a big band and I got a chance to play solos here and there. I became aware of the difference between an artist and a sideman when I began, I was a panelist for the National Endowment for the Arts. First of all I was aware this was not the National Endowment for the Sidemen. It was the National Endowment for the Arts. So in order to be funded by it, it’s to fund artists. So you have to look at yourself as an artist. And then really go to a dictionary and find out what an artist really is if you don’t know. And that’s what I would suggest because that’s one of those words kind of thrown around you know. Everybody’s an artist. You know you draw scratches on the sidewalk and you’re an artist. Anyway, I define artist, the way I defined artist was it’s a person who shows responsibility, you have a responsibility to act like an artist if you’re going to be an artist. And then you have to find out who do you think is an artist. And check out their behavior and so forth. And I don’t know, if you said an artist is Sammy Davis Jr. Check to see his demeanor and manner. You don’t hear him cursing in front of people.

You know Madonna was signed to a contract for 60 million dollars here about a year ago. And I don’t begrudge people their success, but I, when, you know I’ve won some cultural grants. And whenever I won a grant, at the end of the grant period I have to fill out all these things about how I spent the money and what I did and how it helped the community and what kind of people it reached and who I hired. I have to account for every dollar. You know what I mean? And I would just like to see there be some sense of

accountability if people are going to be paid that much money, what are they actually doing, giving back to a community? You know what I mean? And we’ll kind of pick up there. We were talking about the concept of being an artist, and how that can be consistent with, but not always the same as an entertainer. To entertain can merely mean to hold your interest. And that can be done through very positive means or very macabre or very sensational means that don’t have a lot to do with the craft of your art.
